bib.title: Empirical Bayes Estimation Strategies (Computer Age Statistical Inference, ch. 21)

question: How can the prior density g(theta) be learned from many parallel observations (Bayes deconvolution), and how do g-modeling and f-modeling compare?
contributions: Parametric g-modeling: exponential-family prior on a discrete grid, penalized MLE, delta-method and parametric-bootstrap accuracy
Extension to generalized linear mixed models with covariates
Comparison with f-modeling, including the Fourier (sinc kernel) deconvolution method

results.claim: In the prostate data (N=6033 genes), g-modeling estimates the null probability at 0.946, versus 0.984 from locfdr f-modeling.
results.setup: Prostate study, n=102 men, z_i ~ N(mu_i, sigma0^2) with sigma0=1.06; Q = delta at 0 plus 5-df natural spline, T=(-3.6,-3.4,...,3.6); penalized MLE c0=1
results.quote:
Here g-modeling estimated less prior null probability, 0.946 compared
with 0.984 from f -modeling

results.claim: g-modeling estimate of Pr{|mu|>=2} in the prostate data is 0.020 with se 0.0014, implying about 121 genes.
results.setup: Same prostate g-model; se from Theorem 21.4
results.note: 0.020*6033 = 121; sign/inequality symbols dropped in text layer for (21.52), read from text 'About 2% of the genes are estimated to have effect sizes |mu_i|>=2'

results.claim: In the artificial microarray example, g-modeling recovers the null probability 0.891 (true 0.9) with se 0.006.
results.setup: N=10,000 z_i ~ N(mu_i,1); 9000 mu=0, 1000 mu~N(-3,1); T=(-6,-5.75,...,3); spike-and-slab Q (delta at 0 + degree-5 polynomial); penalized MLE c0=1; bias estimate 0.001
results.note: Value 0.891 +/- 0.006 printed as (21.46); recorded in claim only because the equation text is garbled

results.claim: Delta-method standard errors were about 25% too small on the artificial g example, while on the nodes example delta and bootstrap agree closely.
results.setup: Artificial g (1/8 uniform[-3,3] + 7/8 N(0,0.5^2)), N=1000, X~N(theta,1), natural spline df=5, bootstrap B=500; nodes example bootstrap B=1000
results.quote: In this case the delta method standard errors were about 25% too small.

results.claim: Nonparametric Fourier f-modeling had sd of g-hat averaging more than 20 times that of g-modeling at similar bias.
results.setup: Artificial example, N=1000, X~N(theta,1), sinc-kernel lambda=1/3, g-model with ns df=5

results.claim: Parametric f-modeling (Poisson regression on ns df=5) before Fourier deconvolution reduces sd substantially but does not reach g-modeling rates.
results.quote:
We see a substantial decrease in standard deviation, though still not attain-
ing g-modeling rates.

limits: Delta-method accuracy was poor on the artificial example (about 25% too small).
Deficiency of parametric g-modeling: definitional bias when the true g is not in the chosen exponential family (Fig 21.3).
Estimated slab density is only roughly accurate (Fig 21.6) and prostate non-null density estimates have poor accuracy (Fig 21.8).
E{theta|x} is the favorable case; results are worse for other conditional estimates such as E{theta^2|x}.
Fourier method applies only to X = theta + iid noise.
Simplified exposition assumes discrete finite theta and x spaces and a kernel p(x|theta) independent of i.
No code is given; numerical maximizer was nlm in R.
practices: Add a small penalty c0*||alpha|| (c0=1) to the g-model likelihood to avoid corner local maxima (p.428).
Use the parametric bootstrap (resample y ~ Multinomial(N, f(alpha-hat)), start nlm at alpha-hat) when delta-method accuracy is in doubt (p.429-430).
Use f-modeling when the target is expressible in f (Robbins, fdr, Tweedie); use g-modeling when the prior g itself is wanted (p.442).
Treat the assumed Bayes prior as a substantial assumption, not a casual choice (p.443-444).
